It's Not the Shots: What People With Diabetes Say Is Actually the Hardest Part

13 min read · August 2026 · Little Wins Health

What's in this guide

  • The relentless mental load
  • When distress becomes burnout
  • The sleep you lose
  • The loss of spontaneity
  • The cost and the system
  • Judgment and unwanted advice
  • The fear of complications
  • Devices, self-image, and intimacy

"I could never give myself shots" is the line most people reach for when they imagine having diabetes, generally said with a small wince. It's meant kindly, and it fixes on the one part of the condition that's easy to picture from the outside, which is the needle.

People who live with diabetes tend to have a very different answer about which part is the hard one. Ask them, and the injection is rarely where they land.

In one large online conversation, members of a type 1 community were asked what the worst part of the condition was. The person who started it set the needles aside right away, and hundreds of replies followed without mentioning injections at all.

What came up instead was quieter and much harder to see from the outside. People talked about the money it takes, and about the sleep they lose to blood sugars that won't settle at night.

They described the mental math that never fully switches off, and the reactions of other people, like the stranger who answers a diagnosis with a story about a relative who lost a foot. These are the things that wear a person down over the years, and most of them stay invisible to anyone who doesn't live them.

This article is about those answers, the ones that rarely make it into a pamphlet or a first appointment. Most of them apply to both type 1 and type 2 diabetes, though a few differ depending on the type, and we'll flag those where they change the picture.

The honest truth

Here's what surprises people. For most people with diabetes, the injections stop being the hard part pretty fast. What gets you is the stuff nobody sees, the money, the sleep you lose, the mental math that never stops, and everyone else's opinions about a condition they don't have. It's the same story for type 1 and type 2.

Why "I Could Never Give Myself Shots" Misses What's Actually Hard

The comment comes from a kind place, and it's worth taking seriously before setting it aside. Some people have a real fear of needles, which affects around 1 in 10 people, and for them the first injections can be hard. That fear is common enough that there's step-by-step help for needle anxiety, and it generally eases with time and support.

For most people, though, the shot stops being the hard part quite quickly. You have to do it, so you learn how, and something that seemed impossible at first turns into a quick, ordinary habit you barely think about.

This is the part outsiders miss. An injection is easy to notice, so that's what people focus on, while the parts that make diabetes hard happen quietly, out of sight. The hardest parts are the ones no one else can see.

A person with type 1 diabetes needs insulin every day to stay alive, and many people with type 2 use it too. For millions of people, taking insulin is just a normal part of the day, like any other small routine. The real weight comes from everything around that routine, and that's what the rest of this article looks at.

The Relentless Mental Load, and Why Doctors Call It Diabetes Distress

Diabetes never really takes a day off. Every meal needs a rough carb count, and simple choices like going for a walk or eating a snack turn into decisions that can push your blood sugar up or down.

So a big part of living with diabetes happens in your head. You're doing quiet math all day, checking numbers and planning ahead for what your body might do next, and it keeps running in the background even when nothing is wrong.

When that load piles up, it has a name. Doctors call it diabetes distress, the worn-down, overwhelmed state that comes from managing a condition that asks something of you every single day. It's common, and by some estimates it reaches up to 40% of people with diabetes at some point.

One of the most tiring parts is that effort doesn't always show up in the numbers. You can do everything the same two days in a row, the same meal and the same dose, and still end up with two completely different results.

Doing everything right and still getting a bad number is discouraging, and it wears people down over time. Diabetes distress is a normal, understandable response to a hard, non-stop job, and plenty of people who manage their diabetes well still go through it.

When Diabetes Distress Hardens Into Diabetes Burnout

Distress and burnout sound similar, but they're not quite the same thing. Distress is the emotional strain of managing diabetes. Burnout is what can happen when that strain goes on so long that a person starts pulling back from their own care.

In burnout, the everyday tasks start to feel pointless. Someone might check their blood sugar less often and start skipping doses or appointments.

People going through this still know their care is important. They're just too worn out to keep it up the way they want to, and that exhaustion is real.

Because the signs show up as missed checks and skipped doses, people in burnout are sometimes wrongly seen as careless or lazy. But diabetes burnout is a recognized state that many people reach, and it says nothing about how much someone cares.

The good news is that burnout doesn't have to last. It can lift with the right support, like a simpler routine for a while and help from a doctor or diabetes team who understands it. Hitting this wall is something many people with diabetes go through, and with help, it's something they come back from.

The Sleep You Lose to Nighttime Blood Sugar Swings and Alarms

For a lot of people with diabetes, a full night of sleep is rare. Blood sugar can drift too low or climb too high overnight, and either one can pull you out of sleep to deal with it.

If you use a continuous glucose monitor or a pump, the alarms add to it. They're there to keep you safe, and they do, but a device that beeps at 3 a.m. still pulls you awake.

Do this for years and the tiredness builds. Losing sleep night after night makes the next day harder, from focusing at work to managing blood sugar itself, which can then disturb the following night's sleep.

Family members lose sleep too. Parents of children with type 1 often wake through the night to check their child's blood sugar, carrying the worry so their kid can rest.

None of this shows up when people picture life with diabetes. The exhaustion is one of the heaviest parts, and it's mostly invisible to everyone who sleeps through the night.

The Quiet Loss of Spontaneity, From a Snack to an Overnight Trip

A lot of small freedoms quietly disappear with diabetes. You can't always grab a snack or say yes to a last-minute plan without thinking it through first.

Food stops being simple. A slice of cake or a spur-of-the-moment meal out means working out the carbs and the dose, and getting it wrong can mean hours of feeling unwell afterward.

Leaving the house takes planning too. Even a short trip can mean packing insulin, snacks for a low, backup supplies, and a plan for if something goes wrong.

It reaches into major life choices too. Some people hold back from moving abroad or taking certain jobs, because losing access to their medication and supplies is a real risk.

This is hard to explain to someone who has never had to plan their life around a medical condition. The freedom to be spontaneous is something diabetes quietly takes, and its absence shows up in ordinary moments every day.

The Money It Costs, and the Grind of the System Behind Every Refill

For many people, diabetes is expensive to live with. In the United States, care for a person with diabetes runs into thousands of dollars a year, and people with diabetes account for one in four health care dollars spent in the country.

How much of that falls on you depends a lot on where you live. In countries with universal health coverage, most of the cost is carried by the system, while in others people pay a large share out of their own pocket.

When the price is high, some people are pushed into dangerous choices. Around one in four people who use insulin have rationed it because of the cost, which can be life-threatening.

The money is only half of it. There's also the time and effort of dealing with the system, like a pharmacy that fills a prescription wrong or supplies that don't turn up when they should.

Chasing all of this takes hours that most people never see, on top of everything else. For a lot of people, the paperwork and phone calls are as draining as the condition itself.

The Judgment and Unwanted Advice That Come From Everyone Else

Some of the hardest parts of diabetes come from other people. Living with it means fielding a constant stream of comments and advice, most of it unasked for.

There's the person who tells you what you can and can't eat, and the one who's sure that cinnamon or a new diet will fix everything. There's also the stranger who hears "diabetes" and launches into a story about a relative who lost a foot.

What stings is that diabetes often gets judgment where other health conditions get sympathy. If your blood sugar runs high or you end up in the hospital, people can react as though you brought it on yourself.

This is common and well documented. A UK survey found that most people with diabetes have faced blame or judgment, around 86% of those with type 1 and 75% of those with type 2.

The judgment shows up a little differently depending on the type. People with type 2 are often blamed directly for causing their diabetes, while those with type 1 get caught up in the same assumptions through confusion about the two.

Almost none of this is meant to be cruel, but it adds up. Having to explain and brush off other people's opinions becomes its own daily job.

The Fear of Complications and of What the Future Might Hold

Under all the daily tasks sits a quieter worry about the future. Diabetes can lead to serious problems over time, like damage to the eyes, nerves, kidneys, and heart, and most people living with it are aware of that.

That knowledge can weigh on you. Many people carry a low background fear of losing their sight or their independence one day, even when things are going well.

For people with type 1, there's an added fear that comes with depending on insulin to stay alive. Some also run into practical reminders, like being turned down for life insurance, that make the worry harder to set aside.

Here's the part that often gets lost in the fear. Good management lowers the risk of these problems a great deal, and looking after your blood sugar and overall health can prevent or delay many of them.

The fear is real, and it deserves to be taken seriously rather than brushed aside. Living with that uncertainty and getting on with life anyway takes a quiet kind of courage that most people never notice.

How Visible Devices Affect Self-Image and Intimacy

Diabetes technology has made managing blood sugar much easier, but wearing it around the clock can affect how people feel about their bodies. A sensor on the arm or a pump clipped to your waistband is visible, and not everyone is comfortable having it on show.

Some people are self-conscious about the devices, especially in moments like wearing swimwear or meeting someone new. It can take time to make peace with having visible medical gear as part of how you look.

Intimacy can be affected too. A pump or sensor is one more thing to think about, and a low blood sugar can interrupt a moment and call for a pause to treat it.

For most people, this settles with time, and a caring partner takes it in their stride. The technology that keeps you well can also leave you feeling exposed, and getting used to that is a real part of living with diabetes.

What Genuinely Helps When the Load Becomes Too Much

If any of this sounds familiar, the most important thing to know is that help exists and reaching for it works. The daily load is real, and you don't have to carry all of it alone.

Telling your doctor or diabetes team how you're really doing, not just your numbers, can change things. They can screen for diabetes distress and point you toward counseling or other support if that would help.

Other people who live with diabetes can help just as much. Online communities and local groups are full of people who understand the daily reality, and that shared understanding lifts a lot of the weight.

It also helps to ease up on the pressure to be perfect. A simpler routine you can keep up beats an ideal one that burns you out, and being kind to yourself on the hard days is part of good care. Asking for help with the hard parts is a normal, sensible part of managing diabetes, and it often makes everything else easier to carry.

If the emotional side is weighing on you, our guide to diabetes and mental health goes deeper into the support that can help.

You don't have to carry this alone

If the weight of diabetes is getting heavy, tell your diabetes team or your doctor how you're really doing. They can help, and a diabetes helpline or a peer support group can give you somewhere to turn when you need it.

The Hardest Part Is Usually the Part No One Else Can See

Ask people with diabetes what the hardest part is, and they rarely point to the needles. They talk about the sleepless nights, the constant mental load, the cost, and the way other people respond.

What ties those together is that almost none of it is visible from the outside. The hardest parts of diabetes are carried quietly, which is exactly why they can weigh so much.

If you live with diabetes, none of what you carry means you're doing it wrong. The relentless, invisible parts are the real work of diabetes, and getting through them day after day is an achievement worth recognizing.

One little win

Next time someone asks how you're doing, try naming one hard part out loud, to a friend or someone who understands. Putting words to the invisible weight is a small step, and it makes it a little easier to carry.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the hardest part of having diabetes?

For most people it's the invisible, constant parts rather than the injections. The mental load, lost sleep, cost, and other people's reactions tend to wear people down far more than the needles do. This holds true across both type 1 and type 2 diabetes.

What is diabetes distress?

Diabetes distress is the worn-down, overwhelmed feeling that comes from managing diabetes every single day. It's common and separate from depression, and it can be helped with support from your care team. By some estimates it reaches up to 40% of people with diabetes at some point.

Is diabetes burnout a real thing?

Yes. Diabetes burnout is a recognized state where the ongoing strain becomes so heavy that someone starts pulling back from their own care, like skipping checks or doses. It's common and doesn't mean a person has stopped caring, and it tends to lift with the right support.

Is the hardest part the same for type 1 and type 2 diabetes?

Much of it overlaps, like the mental load and the fear of complications. The main differences show up in stigma and in some daily specifics. People with type 2 are more often blamed for causing their diabetes, while those with type 1 carry the constant demands of insulin from day one.

How can I support someone with diabetes?

The most helpful thing is often to skip the unsolicited advice and the worst-case stories. Ask how they're really doing, and offer practical help rather than opinions. Small gestures like that mean more than most people realize.
